claim: Snowflake ID: 41-bit millisecond timestamp with custom epoch
quote: time - 41 bits (millisecond precision w/ a custom epoch gives us 69 years)
author: Twitter (ryanking maintainer)
note: Remaining bit is the unused sign bit; 41+10+12 = 63.

claim: Snowflake ID: 10-bit machine id
quote: configured machine id - 10 bits - gives us up to 1024 machines
author: Twitter

claim: Snowflake ID: 12-bit per-ms sequence, so 4096 IDs per ms per machine
quote: sequence number - 12 bits - rolls over every 4096 per machine (with protection to avoid rollover in the same ms)
author: Twitter
note: 4096 per ms per machine is arithmetic from the 12 bits; the README says rollover protection within the same ms.

claim: Snowflake performance requirement
quote: minimum 10k ids per second per process
author: Twitter

claim: Snowflake latency requirement
quote: response rate 2ms (plus network latency)
author: Twitter

claim: IDs must fit in 64 bits
quote: For various reasons, we need to keep our ids under 64bits.
author: Twitter

claim: Uncoordinated generation
quote: For high availability within and across data centers, machines generating ids should not have to coordinate with each other.
author: Twitter

claim: Clock going backwards: Snowflake refuses to generate
quote: snowflake will refuse to generate ids until a time that is after the last time we generated an id.
author: Twitter

claim: Announcement: composition of timestamp, worker number, sequence number
quote: To generate the roughly-sorted 64 bit ids in an uncoordinated manner, we settled on a composition of: timestamp, worker number and sequence number.
author: Ryan King (@rk)
note: Original blog URL engineering.twitter.com/2010/06/announcing-snowflake.html, read via Wayback 2011 snapshot; blog.x.com copy returned 403.

claim: Worker numbers chosen via ZooKeeper
quote: Sequence numbers are per-thread and worker numbers are chosen at startup via zookeeper (though that’s overridable via a config file).
author: Ryan King (@rk)

claim: Alternatives rejected: ticket servers, 128-bit UUIDs, ZooKeeper sequential nodes
quote: We also considered various UUIDs, but all the schemes we could find required 128 bits.
author: Ryan King (@rk)
note: Same post also rejects 'MySQL-based ticket servers ( like flickr uses )' for lacking ordering guarantees.

claim: k-sorted within about 1 second
quote: We’re aiming to keep our k below 1 second, meaning that tweets posted within a second of one another will be within a second of one another in the id space too.
author: Ryan King (@rk)

claim: Bitly scale (2014): clicks and shortens per month
quote: 6 billion clicks a month 600 million shortens a month
author: Todd Hoff (High Scalability), summarising a talk by Sean O'Connor (Bitly)
note: Secondary source: a summary of O'Connor's Bacon conference talk 'Lessons Learned Building Distributed Systems at Bitly', not Bitly's own blog. Stats are given as a bullet list.

claim: Bitly fleet (2014): ~30 of 400 servers serve all external traffic
quote: ~30 servers handle all incoming traffic from the outside world including shortens, redirects, api requests, web ui, etc.
author: Todd Hoff, summarising Sean O'Connor
note: Same post: '400 servers. Not all 400 servers are handling redirects.'

claim: Bitly: redirect is synchronous, click metrics go onto a queue
quote: When a bitly link is clicked on it’s translated and returned via HTTP. Data about the conversion is popped onto a queue for the analytics and other downstream systems.
author: Todd Hoff, summarising Sean O'Connor

claim: Bitly: shortening must be synchronous for consistency
quote: Don’t want to give out the same shortened URL to multiple users. Rather give an error than a link that doesn’t work.
author: Todd Hoff, summarising Sean O'Connor

claim: Bitly: one click event fans out to multiple consumers
quote: When a bitly URL is decoded into an HTTP redirect a message is sent to multiple services: an archive services that saves it to HDFS and S3, a real-time analytics service, longer term history analytics, an annotation service.
author: Todd Hoff, summarising Sean O'Connor
note: Messaging system named in the post: NSQ ('The real time distributed messaging system bitly uses is Nsq').

claim: Bitly's money is analytics, not shortening
quote: bitly makes money on an analytics product that mashes URL click data with with data they crawl from the web
author: Todd Hoff, summarising Sean O'Connor
note: Typo 'with with' is in the original.

claim: 301 semantics
quote: The 301 (Moved Permanently) status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs.
author: R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke (eds.)

claim: 301 is cacheable by default (heuristically)
quote: A 301 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls (see Section 4.2.2 of [CACHING]).
author: RFC 9110 editors

claim: 302 semantics: client keeps using the original URI
quote: The 302 (Found) status code indicates that the target resource resides temporarily under a different URI. Since the redirection might be altered on occasion, the client ought to continue to use the target URI for future requests.
author: RFC 9110 editors
note: Unlike 301 and 308, the 302 section has no 'heuristically cacheable' sentence; per Section 15.1 it is not heuristically cacheable.

claim: List of heuristically cacheable status codes (302 and 307 absent)
quote: Responses with status codes that are defined as heuristically cacheable (e.g., 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, and 501 in this specification) can be reused by a cache with heuristic expiration unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls [CACHING]; all other status codes are not heuristically cacheable.
author: RFC 9110 editors

claim: 301/302 may change POST to GET; 307/308 exist to forbid that
quote: For historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request. If this behavior is undesired, the 308 (Permanent Redirect) status code can be used instead.
author: RFC 9110 editors
note: Section 15.4.3 has the same note pointing to 307.

claim: 307 semantics: temporary, method preserved
quote: The 307 (Temporary Redirect) status code indicates that the target resource resides temporarily under a different URI and the user agent MUST NOT change the request method if it performs an automatic redirection to that URI.
author: RFC 9110 editors

claim: 308 is heuristically cacheable like 301
quote: A 308 response is heuristically cacheable; i.e., unless otherwise indicated by the method definition or explicit cache controls (see Section 4.2.2 of [CACHING]).
author: RFC 9110 editors

claim: Bitly in practice returns 301 but limits caching with a short private max-age
quote: HTTP/2 301 ... cache-control: private, max-age=90
author: n/a (live response headers via curl -I)
note: Primary observation, not a published statement. The private, max-age=90 header means shared caches must not store it and browsers reuse it only 90 s, so most clicks still reach Bitly for counting. Also sets a _bit cookie.

claim: Public Bitly statement explaining 301 vs 302 choice for analytics

claim: Stripe runs four limiter types
quote: At Stripe, we operate 4 different types of limiters in production. The first one, the Request Rate Limiter , is by far the most important one.
author: Paul Tarjan
note: The space before the comma is an artifact of the HTML.

claim: Request rate limiter definition and volume
quote: This rate limiter restricts each user to N requests per second.
author: Paul Tarjan
note: Same post: 'It has rejected millions of requests this month alone'.

claim: Concurrent requests limiter
quote: Instead of “You can use our API 1000 times a second”, this rate limiter says “You can only have 20 API requests in progress at the same time”.
author: Paul Tarjan
note: Triggered 'much less often (12,000 requests this month)'.

claim: Fleet usage load shedder: 20% reserved for critical, 503 for the rest
quote: If our reservation number is 20%, then any non-critical request over their 80% allocation would be rejected with status code 503.
author: Paul Tarjan

claim: Worker utilization load shedder: last line, sheds by 4 priority classes
quote: This load shedder is the final line of defense. If your workers start getting backed up with requests, then this will shed lower-priority traffic.
author: Paul Tarjan
note: Classes: Critical methods, POSTs, GETs, Test mode traffic. 'Only 100 requests were rejected this month from this rate limiter'.

claim: Stripe uses token bucket on Redis
quote: We use the token bucket algorithm to do rate limiting. ... We implement our rate limiters using Redis.
author: Paul Tarjan
note: Two sentences joined with ellipsis; both verbatim.

claim: Fail open if the limiter or Redis breaks
quote: Make sure that if there were bugs in the rate limiting code (or if Redis were to go down), requests wouldn’t be affected.
author: Paul Tarjan

claim: Dark launch limiters first
quote: Dark launch each rate limiter to watch the traffic they would block.
author: Paul Tarjan

claim: Gist: token bucket relies on atomic Redis scripts
quote: This uses a basic token bucket algorithm and relies on the fact that Redis scripts execute atomically. No other operations can run between fetching the count and writing the new count.
author: Paul Tarjan
note: Gist example: REPLENISH_RATE = 100, CAPACITY = 5 * REPLENISH_RATE; two Redis keys (tokens, timestamp); comment 'Our observed failure rate is 0.01%.' for Redis errors (fail open).

claim: Gist: concurrency limiter as a Redis set
quote: Because Redis is so fast, doing the naive thing works. Just add a random token to a set at the start of a request and remove it from the set when you're done.
author: Paul Tarjan

claim: Cloudflare sliding window approximation (worked example)
author: Julien Desgats
note: Setup: limit 50 req/min; 18 requests in the current minute which started 15 s ago, 42 in the previous minute. General form: prev * (window - elapsed)/window + current.

claim: Approximation assumption
quote: This algorithm assumes a constant rate of requests during the previous sampling period (which can be any time span), this is why the result is only an approximation of the actual rate.
author: Julien Desgats

claim: Measured error of the approximation
quote: 0.003% of requests have been wrongly allowed or rate limited
author: Julien Desgats
note: Preceded by 'an analysis on 400 million requests from 270,000 distinct sources shown:'; also 'An average difference of 6% between real rate and the approximate rate' and 'None of the mitigated sources was below the threshold (false positives)'.

claim: Only memcache GET, SET, INCR available; two numbers per counter
quote: So the situation was that the only operations available were GET , SET and INCR (atomic increment).
author: Julien Desgats
note: Also 'Tiny memory usage: only two numbers per counter'.

claim: Per-PoP Twemproxy-sharded memcache with consistent hashing
quote: we created a Twemproxy cluster inside each of our PoPs: this allows us to split a memcache [2] database across many servers.
author: Julien Desgats
note: Anycast keeps one IP's traffic in one PoP, so counting is per PoP, not global.

claim: Increments off the request path; mitigation decision cached locally
quote: This is why the increment jobs are run asynchronously without slowing down the requests.
author: Julien Desgats

claim: Cloudflare scale
quote: The rate limiter already handles several billion requests per day and we recently mitigated attacks with as many as 400,000 requests per second to a single domain without degrading service for legitimate users.
author: Julien Desgats

claim: GitHub moved from shared Memcached to replicated, client-sharded Redis
quote: We adopted a replicated Redis backend with client-side sharding.
author: Robert Mosolgo

claim: GitHub design: app-side sharding, primary for writes, replicas for reads, Lua for atomicity
quote: Implement the storage logic in Lua, to guarantee atomicity of operations (this was an improvement over the previous design)
author: Robert Mosolgo
note: Other bullets: 'Shard inside the application', 'put a single primary (for writes) and several replicas (for reads) in each cluster'.

claim: Why they left Memcached: evictions reset limits
quote: when it filled up, it would sometimes evict rate limiter data, even when it was still active.
author: Robert Mosolgo

claim: Replica expiry bug: replicas do not expire keys on their own
quote: replicas don’t expire data until they receive instructions to do so from their primaries, and primaries don’t expire keys until they’re accessed
author: Robert Mosolgo
note: Caused rejections with 'X-RateLimit-Remaining: 5000'. Fix: store expires-at explicitly and avoid a second DB call on rejected requests.

claim: Rollout behind a feature flag
quote: We used a feature flag to gate access to the new backend.
author: Robert Mosolgo

claim: Redis Lua scripts are atomic
quote: Redis guarantees the script's atomic execution. While executing the script, all server activities are blocked during its entire runtime.
author: Redis

claim: Redis INCR doc: 'Pattern: rate limiter'
quote: The rate limiter pattern is a special counter that is used to limit the rate at which an operation can be performed.
author: Redis
note: Rate limiter 1: key ip+':'+ts, MULTI INCR + EXPIRE 10, reject if > 10. Rate limiter 2: single counter with EXPIRE 1, which has a race fixed by a Lua script via EVAL.

claim: INCR + EXPIRE race and the Lua fix
quote: If for some reason the client performs the INCR command but does not perform the EXPIRE the key will be leaked until we'll see the same IP address again.
author: Redis

claim: Envoy ratelimit is a Go/gRPC service backed by Redis
quote: The rate limit service is a Go/gRPC service designed to enable generic rate limit scenarios from different types of applications.
author: envoyproxy/ratelimit maintainers
note: Continues: 'The service reads the configuration from disk via runtime, composes a cache key, and talks to the Redis cache.'

claim: Envoy descriptors
quote: A descriptor is a list of key/value pairs owned by a domain that the Ratelimit service uses to select the correct rate limit to use when limiting.
author: envoyproxy/ratelimit maintainers
note: Examples in README: ("database", "users"); ("to_cluster", "service_a"),("from_cluster", "service_b").
